questions.question_text:
$X\sim N(90,49)$.
What are the mean and the standard deviation of $X$?

options.why: Read the second number as the standard deviation, but it is the variance.
Swapped the two entries, taking the variance as the mean.
Took the square root correctly but then swapped it with the mean.

options.why: Read the variance $0.04$ as the standard deviation.
Found the square root of the variance but swapped it with the mean.

options.why: Swapped the mean and the standard deviation.
Doubled the variance instead of taking its square root.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim N(200,64)$.
What is the z-score for $x=216$?

options.why: Divided $216-200=16$ by the variance $64$ instead of the standard deviation $8$.
Subtracted the score from the mean, calculating $(200-216)/8$.
Divided the score $216$ by $8$ without first subtracting the mean.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim N(140,100)$.
What raw score has a z-score of $-1.5$?

options.why: Used $z=1.5$ instead of $-1.5$, calculating $140+1.5\times10$.
Used the variance $100$ as the standard deviation, calculating $140-1.5\times100$.
Added the z-score directly to the mean without multiplying it by the standard deviation.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim N(48,25)$ and $Y\sim N(300,400)$.
Which pair of scores standardises to the same $z$ value?

options.why: Used one of $Y$'s standard deviations for the increase in $X$, giving $x=48+20=68$ and $z_X=4$, while $y=340$ gives $z_Y=2$.
Used one of $X$'s standard deviations for the increase in $Y$, giving $y=300+5=305$ and $z_Y=0.25$, while $x=58$ gives $z_X=2$.
Added one swapped standard deviation to each mean: $48+20=68$ and $300+5=305$, giving $z_X=4$ and $z_Y=0.25$.

questions.solution_text:
For $X$ the standard deviation is $\sqrt{25}=5$.
$z$
$=\frac{58-48}{5}$
$=2$
For $Y$ the standard deviation is $\sqrt{400}=20$.
$z$
$=\frac{340-300}{20}$
$=2$
The pair $x=58$ and $y=340$ standardises to the same $z$ value.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim N(-6,3^{2})$.
What are the mean and the standard deviation of $X$?

options.why: Evaluated $3^{2}$ and read the answer as the standard deviation rather than the variance.
Dropped the negative sign on the mean, although a normal mean may be negative.
Took the base of the square as the mean and its value as the standard deviation.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim N(40,\sigma^{2})$.
The score $x=58$ standardises to $z=1.5$.
What is $\sigma$?

options.why: Used the difference $58-40$ as the standard deviation without dividing by the z-score.
Multiplied $58-40=18$ by $1.5$ instead of dividing by $1.5$.
Found the standard deviation $12$ but squared it and reported the variance.
